CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: skeletal muscle

3 of 5 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 0 fall below it; 2 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

  • Glycogen: ✓ detectable (rNOE)
  • Carnosine: ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)
  • Mobile Protein (Amide Protons): ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)
  • Taurine: ? unknown (not simulated)
  • Glutamate: ? unknown (not simulated)

Excluded before simulation (not stored in the tissue): [model's own exclusion] Glycosaminoglycans (gagCEST): Not physiologically relevant in skeletal muscle parenchyma (primarily cartilage/disc).; [model's own exclusion] Total Creatine: Rejected as a spectroscopic peak grouping (Creatine + Phosphocreatine). Individual components like Creatine are included if relevant, but Taurine and Carnosine are more distinct small-molecule CEST targets in muscle.; [model's own exclusion] Lipid CH2 / MRS peak groupings: Rejected as not chemically defined CEST targets.

Recommended field strength(s): 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: robust

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (Aliphatic C-H (rNOE) [rnoe]: concentration 80-120 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.29-0.44%, 1.5 T: 1.01-1.50%, 3 T: 1.43-2.13%, 5 T: 2.34-3.47%, 7 T: 2.58-3.83%. Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis: Hydroxyl and rNOE pools are both buried in the semisolid MT tail at all fields. Separation from MT is small compared to MT linewidth. Glycogen rNOE overlaps with macromolecular rNOE background.

Direct water saturation: Direct saturation bandwidth is negligible compared to offsets.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Hydroxyl kex borrowed from mouse phantom. rNOE kex borrowed from generic phantom. Both are likely inaccurate for in vivo human muscle.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.1 µT, Tsat=1500 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.366% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.1 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 1.255% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Slow rNOE exchange peaks at low B1. High B1 causes direct water saturation. Low B1 required.
    recommended sequence: 1.785% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Same as 3T. Slow exchange favors low B1.
    recommended sequence: 2.906% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Same as 3T. Higher field improves ppm resolution but MT width in Hz also grows.
    recommended sequence: 3.207% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: Multi-pool fitting required. MTRasym is insufficient due to MT overlap. See MacKay 2006, Hennessy 2019.

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

hydroxyl (glycoCEST, 0.5-1.5 ppm): 0 CEST/NOE application and 3 metabolite-change studies verified (2 human, 1 animal; 48 humans, 12 animals; 5 dropped by verification). Glycogen CEST (glycoCEST) has been applied to liver in fasting/post-meal states but not specifically to skeletal muscle disease. Metabolite change evidence is strong in metabolic myopathies: glycogen accumulates in Pompe disease (skeletal muscle biopsy) and decreases in type 2 diabetes/severe obesity (biopsy/myotubes). Muscle glycogen is also altered by detraining.

It does not report a single aggregate mean and SD for all disease subjects versus controls. Instead, it reports relative elevations (percentages) for specific age cohorts (e.g., 'At two weeks old... 119% ± 57% elevation', 'plateau phase of 311% ± 48% elevation'). The absolute glycoNOE signal values (mean and SD) for the disease and control groups are not provided in the text, only relative differences or estimated concentrations derived from tissue assays for specific ages. Therefore, disease mean/sd and control mean/sd for the glycoNOE signal (-1 ppm) are null.PMID 39529314

Caveats / critique (7 points, 304 words) — Concentration 100 mM is plausible for resting muscle. However, glycogen is highly dynamic. Static concentration is a poor model without dietary/exercise control…
  • Concentration 100 mM is plausible for resting muscle. However, glycogen is highly dynamic. Static concentration is a poor model without dietary/exercise control. Hydroxyl class correct. rNOE class correct. Hydroxyl kex is extremely high (fast exchange), limiting CEST contrast to line-broadening. Provenance is phantom/mouse.
  • Shifts -1.1 ppm for rNOE and 1.0 ppm for hydroxyl are consistent with literature values in mouse models. None identified. Robustness to input uncertainty: fragile

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (Amide NH [amide]: concentration 15-45 mM, kex 39.17-54.97 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.07-0.22%, 1.5 T: 0.19-0.69%, 3 T: 0.26-0.95%, 5 T: 0.36-1.31%, 7 T: 0.37-1.37%. Threshold 0.5%. Only the point estimate clears the threshold; the low corner does not.

Frequency-collision analysis: Carnosine Amide (3.5 ppm) completely overlaps with Mobile Protein Amide (3.5 ppm). Cannot be resolved by offset alone.

Direct water saturation: Direct saturation negligible at 3.5 ppm.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Amide kex borrowed from phantom solution. In vivo pH affects rate.

Potential clinical impact

imidazole (no established CEST pool): 0 CEST/NOE application and 1 metabolite-change studies verified (1 human, 0 animal; 263 humans, 0 animals; 1 dropped by verification). No CEST applications for carnosine were found. Carnosine can be quantified by 1H-MRS at 7T in skeletal muscle. Content increases during male puberty and decreases from young to middle adulthood, but does not differ significantly between middle-aged and elderly. No specific muscle disease associations were identified.

Potential clinical impact

amide (APT, 3.5 ppm): 0 CEST/NOE application and 2 metabolite-change studies verified (1 human, 1 animal; 0 humans, 8 animals; 2 dropped by verification). No APT MRI applications were found specifically in skeletal muscle disease. However, protein homeostasis is profoundly altered in muscle wasting (sarcopenia/cachexia), inclusion body myopathy (TDP-43 aggregation), muscular dystrophy (ubiquitin-proteasome degradation), and heart failure (elevated proteasome activity). APT could theoretically report on mobile amide protons from these protein aggregates or degraded proteins.

In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — Axial slab through the mid-thigh, centered on the vastus lateralis muscle belly, 10 cm proximal to the femoral condyles.

Why this scan:

  • Skeletal muscle has high concentrations of proteins, glycogen, and carnosine, whereas subcutaneous fat and bone marrow have negligible amounts of these metabolites. By acquiring a Z-spectrum from a single axial slab containing muscle, fat, and marrow, we can distinguish specific metabolite CEST effects from generic background MT/NOE.
  • Background effects will be similar across ROIs (scaled by water content/proton density), whereas specific metabolite signals will appear only in the muscle ROI. This differential approach confirms the tissue-specific origin of any observed contrast.
ROIWhere it is drawnRole
Skeletal Muscle target tissueManual ROI drawn within the vastus lateralis muscle compartment on the axial slice, excluding the femur and subcutaneous fat.Target tissue with high concentrations of mobile protein, glycogen, and carnosine.
Subcutaneous FatManual ROI drawn in the circumferential subcutaneous adipose tissue layer surrounding the thigh muscles.Comparison tissue with negligible protein, glycogen, and carnosine; serves as a negative control for metabolite-specific signals.
Bone MarrowManual ROI drawn in the central medullary cavity of the femur.Comparison tissue with low protein content and negligible glycogen/carnosine; helps characterize baseline MT effects.

Scan protocol: 3 T, pulsed Gaussian train, B1=1.5 µT, 60 pulses × 10 ms (interpulse delay 40 ms, duty cycle 20%), total Tsat=3000 ms, TR=4000 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): At 3T, 1.5 µT with 20% duty cycle yields very low local SAR (< 0.1 W/kg), well within safety limits for extremity/whole-body coils. No heating concerns for muscle tissue.

Compromise rationale: Agent 1 recommended B1=0.5 µT for all three metabolites. We choose 1.5 µT to favor the intermediate-exchange Amide protons (APT, 3.5 ppm), which require higher B1 for efficient saturation. This higher B1 may oversaturate the fast-exchange Carboxyl/Hydroxyl (Glycogen, 0.8 ppm) and Amine (Carnosine, -1.9 ppm) pools, broadening their direct water saturation tails. However, the large concentration differences between muscle and fat/marrow allow us to isolate these signals by subtraction/comparison.

Fat suppression: SPIR prepulse. Used to suppress the strong lipid signal from subcutaneous fat (ROI 2) to prevent lipid tail overlap with CEST signals (especially rNOE/Glycogen) and to improve SNR for the muscle ROI.

Motion mitigation: Subject lies supine. Scan is performed on the thigh (vastus lateralis) to avoid respiratory and cardiac motion. No gating or breath-holds required. Stability is high.

Slice coverage: Single axial slab, 10 mm thick, centered at the mid-thigh level (approx. 10 cm proximal to femoral condyles). Covers the entire cross-section of the thigh including muscle, fat, and bone.

Structures in FOV: Skeletal Muscle (Vastus Lateralis), Subcutaneous Adipose Tissue, Femoral Bone Marrow, Femoral Cortical Bone

Differential analysis plan:

  • For each ROI, compute MTRasym(3.5 ppm) for APT, MTRasym(0.8 ppm) for Glycogen, and MTRasym(2.3 ppm) for Carnosine. We expect: 1) APT (3.5 ppm) to be strong in Muscle, weak in Marrow, negligible in Fat. 2) Glycogen (0.8 ppm) and Carnosine (2.3 ppm) signals to be present only in Muscle.
  • 3) Any contrast appearing in Fat/Marrow at these offsets is attributed to background MT/NOE or B0/B1 inhomogeneity. Confirmation requires Muscle signal to be significantly higher than Fat/Marrow, with the differential pattern matching the known concentration gradients.

Not actively targeted: Taurine and Glutamate were excluded because their simulated contrast at 3 T was negligible (<0.1%), making them undetectable with this practical scan time and B1 constraints.

Caveats (7 points, 322 words) — Partial volume effects in the 10 mm slice may dilute muscle signal if the ROI is too small. B0 inhomogeneity across the thigh (due to air-muscle interfaces) req…
  • Partial volume effects in the 10 mm slice may dilute muscle signal if the ROI is too small. B0 inhomogeneity across the thigh (due to air-muscle interfaces) requires careful WASSR correction. B1 inhomogeneity may cause the 1.5 µT compromise to under-saturate fast-exchange pools (Glycogen/Carnosine) in some regions.
  • The high B1 may also introduce direct water saturation tails that mimic CEST effects.
